SOMERVILLE, Tenn. Here in Fayette County, Negroes are winning on the political front but losing on the economic one.
This is the county where evicted Negro farmers lived in tents three years ago to establish the right to register and vote.
They have established that right now. In 1959, there were only about 50 Negro voters in this county. Today there are close to 4,000 more than the registered white voters in the county.
The same picture is developing in neighboring Haywood County, where there were virtually no Negro voters three years ago and where there are now well over 2,000. Negroes outnumber whites in both these counties in the southwest corner of Tennessee, where conditions are very similar to those in neighboring Mississippi.
But despite the new voting strength, the Negroes here are not free. When young demonstrators sat in and demanded a beginning of desegregation this summer, they were met with arrests and mob violence. John McFerren, Fayette County Negro leader, who organized the civil-rights drive here and still heads it, explains: The economic squeeze is worse than ever; they just go about it in a quiet way now.

Since its founding in 1939 in the Library of Benedict College in Columbia, the South Carolina Conference of Branches, NAACP has played a major role in the Civii Rights Struggle in South Carolina. In the 1940's the South Carolina Conference of Branches, NAACP was active in obtaining equalization of teachers' salaries and breaking segregation barriers in the all-white South Carolina Democratic primary. Milestones of the 40's include: 1941: J. M. Hinton elected State Conference President. 1944: NAACP asks courts for voting rights of South Carolina Negroes. 1947: NAACP breaks segregation barrier in South Carolina Democratic Primary.
